metadata.title: A Short Proof of Bernoulli Disjointness via the Local Lemma

nodes.name: Standing assumptions
nodes.statement: Throughout, $\G$ denotes an infinite discrete \ep{but not necessarily countable} group. All topological spaces in this paper are assumed to be Hausdorff.

nodes.name: $\G$-flow
nodes.statement: A \emphd{$\G$-flow} is a nonempty compact space $X$ equipped with a continuous action $\G \acts X$.

nodes.name: subflow
nodes.statement: A \emphd{subflow} of a $\G$-flow $X$ is a nonempty closed $\G$-invariant subset $Y \subseteq X$.

nodes.name: minimal $\G$-flow
nodes.statement: A $\G$-flow $X$ is \emphd{minimal} if there is no subflow $Y \subseteq X$ with $Y \neq X$; equivalently, $X$ is minimal if the orbit of every point $x \in X$ is dense in $X$.
differentia: there is no subflow $Y \subseteq X$ with $Y \neq X$

nodes.name: Existence of minimal subflows (Zorn's Lemma)
nodes.statement: A straightforward application of Zorn's lemma shows that every $\G$-flow has a minimal subflow. This demonstrates that minimal flows \emph{exist}, but in general it is very difficult to say much about their structure and behavior.

nodes.name: Bernoulli shift
nodes.statement:
Let $X$ be a nonempty compact space. The space $X^\G$ of all functions $\G\to X$, equipped with the product topology, is also compact, and it becomes a $\G$-flow under the action $\G \acts X^\G$ given by
	\[
		(\gamma \cdot x)(\delta) \,\defeq\, x(\delta\gamma) \qquad \text{for all $\gamma$, $\delta \in \G$ and $x \in X^\G$}.
	\]
	The $\G$-flows of the form $X^\G$ are called \emphd{Bernoulli shifts}, or simply \emphd{shifts}.

nodes.name: Finite alphabet convention ($X=k$)
nodes.statement: A particularly important case is when $X$ is a finite set with the discrete topology; for concreteness, we may then assume that $X = k$ for some $k \in \N$. \ep{Here we identify each $k \in \N$ with the $k$-element set $\set{i \in \N \,:\, i < k}$.}

nodes.name: Attribution: joining and disjointness (Furstenberg)
nodes.statement: The following notions were introduced by Furstenberg in \cite{Furstenberg}.

nodes.name: joining
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be $\G$-flows. We view the product space $X \times Y$ as a $\G$-flow equipped with the diagonal action of $\G$. A \emphd{joining} of $X$ and $Y$ is a subflow $Z \subseteq X \times Y$ that projects onto $X$ and $Y$.

nodes.name: disjoint $\G$-flows ($X \perp Y$)
nodes.statement: The $\G$-flows $X$ and $Y$ are \emphd{disjoint}, in symbols $X \perp Y$, if they have only one joining, namely $X \times Y$ itself.

nodes.name: Disjointness implies one factor minimal
nodes.statement: It is not hard to see that if $X \perp Y$, then at least one of $X$ and $Y$ is minimal.

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (Glasner–Tsankov–Weiss–Zucker)
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a minimal $\G$-flow, then $X \perp 2^\G$.
nodes.label: theo:disj

nodes.name: Furstenberg's proof for $\G=\Z$
nodes.statement: For $\G = \Z$, Theorem~\ref{theo:disj} was proven earlier by Furstenberg \cite{Furstenberg}.

nodes.name: GTWZ's group-theoretic proof strategy
nodes.statement: The first step in the proof of Theorem~\ref{theo:disj} in \cite{GTWZ} is a reduction to a combinatorial question concerning the so-called \emph{separated covering property} of minimal $\G$-flows. Somewhat surprisingly, to answer this question, \cite{GTWZ} makes heavy use of group theory; in particular, two classes of groups \ep{namely \emph{maximally almost periodic} and \emph{ICC} groups} are treated separately and with completely different arguments. The proof in the ICC case relies on the recent breakthrough results of Frisch, Tamuz, and Vahidi Ferdowsi \cite{FTF}.

nodes.name: This paper's proof strategy (overview)
nodes.statement: In this note, we give a short and self-contained proof of Theorem~\ref{theo:disj} that is purely combinatorial and treats all groups simultaneously. We deduce Theorem~\ref{theo:disj} from the following fact, which is interesting in its own right.

nodes.name: traps / trapped
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a $\G$-flow. We say that a set $U \subseteq X$ \emphd{traps} a point $x \in X$ \ep{or that $x$ is \emphd{trapped} in $U$} if the orbit of $x$ is contained in $U$.

nodes.name: Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let $k \in \N^+$ and let $V \subseteq k^\G$ be a nonempty open set. Then there exists $n \in \N$ such that for all finite $F \subset \G$ of size at least $n$, the set $F \cdot V$ traps a point.
nodes.statement_short: Every nonempty open $V\subseteq k^\G$ is trapped by $F\cdot V$ for all large enough finite $F\subset\G$.
assumptions: $V \subseteq k^\G$ be a nonempty open set
conclusions: there exists $n \in \N$ such that for all finite $F \subset \G$ of size at least $n$, the set $F \cdot V$ traps a point
nodes.label: theo:synd

nodes.name: Roadmap of the paper
nodes.statement:
Theorem~\ref{theo:disj} is derived from Theorem~\ref{theo:synd} in \S\ref{sec:reduction}. To establish Theorem~\ref{theo:synd}, we rely on the so-called \emph{Lov\'asz Local Lemma} \ep{the \emph{LLL} for short}, an important tool in probabilistic combinatorics introduced by Erd\H{o}s and Lov\'asz in \cite{EL}.
	We state the LLL, in the form we will need, in \S\ref{sec:LLL} and use it to prove Theorem~\ref{theo:synd} in \S\ref{sec:synd}. While the LLL has been widely used in combinatorics and graph theory for over forty years now, it has only recently become apparent that the LLL can be applied to the study of dynamical systems as well. Several applications of the LLL in ergodic theory and topological dynamics can be found in \cite{ABT, LSS, MLLL, AW}; this paper contributes yet another one.

nodes.name: Recurrence Lemma
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a minimal $\G$-flow and $U \subseteq X$ is a nonempty open set, then there exists an infinite subset $S \subseteq \G$ with $\bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in S} \neq \0$.
assumptions: $U \subseteq X$ is a nonempty open set
conclusions: there exists an infinite subset $S \subseteq \G$ with $\bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in S} \neq \0$
nodes.label: lemma:rec

nodes.name: Proof of the Recurrence Lemma
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is minimal, the orbit of each point in $X$ intersects $U$, and thus $X = \G \cdot U$. The compactness of $X$ implies that there is a finite subset $T \subset \G$ such that $X = T \cdot U$. Say that a set $L \subseteq \G$ is \emphd{right $T$-separated} if $\lambda_1T \cap \lambda_2T = \0$ for every pair of distinct $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2 \in L$. Since $T$ is finite while $\G$ is infinite, there is an infinite right $T$-separated subset $L \subseteq \G$. Consider any $x \in U$. For each $\lambda \in L$, we have $\lambda^{-1} \cdot x \in T \cdot U$, i.e., $x \in \lambda T \cdot U$. In other words, for each $\lambda \in L$, there is $\tau_\lambda \in T$ with $x \in \lambda \tau_\lambda \cdot U$. Since $L$ is right $T$-separated, the set $S \defeq \set{\lambda \tau_\lambda \,:\, \lambda \in L}$ is infinite, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness gives a finite covering set $T$; a right $T$-separated infinite set yields the recurrence set $S$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
Let $X$ be a minimal $\G$-flow and let $Z \subseteq X \times 2^\G$ be a joining. Our goal is to show that $Z = X \times 2^\G$. To this end, let $U \subseteq X$ and $V \subseteq 2^\G$ be nonempty open sets. We have to argue that $Z \cap (U \times V) \neq \0$.
	
	\begin{lemma}
		If $X$ is a minimal $\G$-flow and $U \subseteq X$ is a nonempty open set, then there exists an infinite subset $S \subseteq \G$ with $\bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in S} \neq \0$.
	\end{lemma}
	\begin{scproof}
		Since $X$ is minimal, the orbit of each point in $X$ intersects $U$, and thus $X = \G \cdot U$. The compactness of $X$ implies that there is a finite subset $T \subset \G$ such that $X = T \cdot U$. Say that a set $L \subseteq \G$ is \emphd{right $T$-separated} if $\lambda_1T \cap \lambda_2T = \0$ for every pair of distinct $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2 \in L$. Since $T$ is finite while $\G$ is infinite, there is an infinite right $T$-separated subset $L \subseteq \G$. Consider any $x \in U$. For each $\lambda \in L$, we have $\lambda^{-1} \cdot x \in T \cdot U$, i.e., $x \in \lambda T \cdot U$. In other words, for each $\lambda \in L$, there is $\tau_\lambda \in T$ with $x \in \lambda \tau_\lambda \cdot U$. Since $L$ is right $T$-separated, the set $S \defeq \set{\lambda \tau_\lambda \,:\, \lambda \in L}$ is infinite, and we are done. 
	\end{scproof}
	
	Let $S \subseteq \G$ be an infinite set as in Lemma~\ref{lemma:rec} applied to $U$, and let $n \in \N$ be the quantity given by Theorem~\ref{theo:synd} applied to $V$. Pick an arbitrary finite subset $F \subset S$ of size at least $n$ and let
	\[
	U^\ast \,\defeq\, \bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in F}.
	\]
	By the choice of $n$, the set $F \cdot V$ traps a point, say $y$. Since $Z$ projects onto $2^\G$, there is some $x \in X$ with $(x,y) \in Z$. As $X$ is minimal and $U^\ast$ is nonempty open, there is $\gamma \in \G$ with $\gamma \cdot x \in U^\ast$. Since $y$ is trapped in $F \cdot V$, we have $\gamma \cdot y \in F \cdot V$, which means that $\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot y \in V$ for some $\sigma \in F$, and since $\gamma \cdot x \in U^\ast$, we also have $\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot x \in U$. Therefore,
	\[
	(\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot x, \, \sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot y) \,=\, \sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot (x,y) \,\in\, Z \cap (U \times V),
	\]
	and the proof of Theorem~\ref{theo:disj} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Recurrence Lemma to $U$ and Theorem 2 to $V$, then combine the resulting group elements to hit $Z\cap(U\times V)$.

nodes.name: Scope of the LLL version used
nodes.statement: We shall only require a somewhat specialized but simplified version of the Lov\'asz Local Lemma; for a more general discussion of the LLL, the reader is referred to~\cite{AS} and \cite{MR}. The presentation below follows, with slight modifications,~\cite[\S{}1.2]{MLLL}.

nodes.name: bad ($k$-)event
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an arbitrary set and let $k \in \N^+$. A \emphd{bad \ep{$k$-}event} over $X$ is a nonempty set $B$ of partial functions $\phi \colon X \rightharpoonup k$ with finite domains such that for all $\phi$, $\phi' \in B$, $\dom(\phi) = \dom(\phi')$.
nodes.genus: nonempty set $B$ of partial functions $\phi \colon X \rightharpoonup k$ with finite domains

nodes.name: domain of a bad event
nodes.statement: If a bad event $B$ is nonempty, then its \emphd{domain} is the set $\dom(B) \coloneqq \dom(\phi)$ for any \ep{hence all} $\phi \in B$; the domain of the empty bad event is, by definition, the empty set.

nodes.name: probability of a bad event
nodes.statement: The \emphd{probability} of a bad $k$-event $B$ with domain $D$ is defined to be $\P[B] \coloneqq |B|/k^{|D|}$.

nodes.name: avoids
nodes.statement: A map $f \colon X \to k$ \emphd{avoids} a bad event $B$ if there is no $\phi \in B$ such that $\phi \subseteq f$.

nodes.name: Interpretation of $\P[B]$
nodes.statement: Notice that if $X$ is finite and $f \colon X \to k$ is drawn uniformly at random from $k^X$, then $\P[B]$ is precisely the probability that $f$ \emph{does not} avoid $B$.

nodes.name: ($k$-)instance of the LLL
nodes.statement: A~\emphd{\ep{$k$\=/}instance \ep{of the LLL}} over a set $X$ is an arbitrary set $\B$ of bad $k$-events over $X$.

nodes.name: solution (to an LLL instance)
nodes.statement: A~\emphd{solution} to a $k$-instance~$\B$ is a function $f \colon X \to k$ that avoids every $B \in \B$.

nodes.name: neighborhood $N_\B(B)$
nodes.statement:
For an instance $\B$ and $B \in \B$, the \emphd{neighborhood} of $B$ in $\B$ is the set
	\[
	\Nbhd_\B(B) \defeq \set{B' \in \B \setminus \set{B} \,:\, \dom(B') \cap \dom(B) \neq \0}.

nodes.name: degree $\deg_\B(B)$
nodes.statement: The \emphd{degree} of $B$ in $\B$ is defined to be $\deg_\B(B) \defeq |\Nbhd_\B(B)|$.

nodes.name: $p(\B)$ and $d(\B)$
nodes.statement:
Let
	\[
	p(\B) \defeq \sup_{B \in \B} \P[B] \qquad \text{and} \qquad d(\B) \defeq \sup_{B \in \B} \deg_\B(B).
	\]

nodes.name: correct for the LLL
nodes.statement:
An instance $\B$ is \emphd{correct for the LLL}, or simply \emphd{correct}, if
	\[
	e\cdot p(\B) \cdot (d(\B) + 1) < 1,
	\]
	where $e = 2.71\ldots${} denotes the base of the natural logarithm.

nodes.name: Lovász Local Lemma (Erdős–Lovász)
nodes.statement: Let $k \in \N^+$ and let $\B$ be a $k$-instance of the LLL over a set $X$. If $\B$ is correct for the LLL, then $\B$ has a solution.
assumptions: $\B$ be a $k$-instance of the LLL over a set $X$
nodes.label: theo:LLL

nodes.name: History of the LLL constant
nodes.statement: The LLL was introduced by Erd\H os and Lov\'asz \ep{with $4$ in place of $e$} in their seminal paper~\cite{EL}; the constant was subsequently improved by Lov\'asz (the sharpened version first appeared in~\cite{Spencer}).

nodes.name: Scope note: product probability spaces
nodes.statement:
We should mention that there are two respects in which Theorem~\ref{theo:LLL} in the above form is less general then the ``full'' LLL. First, Theorem~\ref{theo:LLL} only works with \emph{product} probability spaces such as $k^X$; this is a special case of the~LLL in the so-called \emph{variable framework} (the~name is due to Kolipaka and Szegedy~\cite{KolipakaSzegedy}).
	However, although this case is special, it does encompass most typical applications. For the statement of the~LLL for general probability spaces, see~\cite[Corollary~5.1.2]{AS}. Deducing Theorem~\ref{theo:LLL} from \cite[Corollary~5.1.2]{AS} is routine when $X$ is finite (see, e.g., \cite[41]{MR}); the case of infinite~$X$ then follows by compactness.

nodes.name: Scope note: General Lovász Local Lemma
nodes.statement: Second, there is a more general form of the LLL \ep{often referred to as the \emph{General Lov\'asz Local Lemma}}, that applies to instances without a uniform upper bound on $\deg_\B(B)$; see \cite[Theorem 5.1.1]{AS}. However, this more general statement is somewhat technical and we will not need it here.

nodes.name: left $D$-separated
nodes.statement: Let $D \subset \G$ be a finite set. We say that a set $L \subseteq \G$ is \emphd{left $D$-separated} if $D\lambda_1 \cap D\lambda_2 = \0$ for every pair of distinct $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2 \in L$.

nodes.name: Independent Set Lemma
nodes.statement: If $D$, $F \subset \G$ are finite sets, then $F$ has a left $D$-separated subset $L \subseteq F$ with \[|L| \geq |F|/|D|^2.\]
conclusions: $F$ has a left $D$-separated subset $L \subseteq F$ with \[|L| \geq |F|/|D|^2.\]
nodes.label: lemma:indep

nodes.name: Proof of the Independent Set Lemma
nodes.statement: First recall some basic facts about finite graphs. Let $G$ be a finite graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$. A subset $I \subseteq V$ is \emphd{independent \ep{in $G$}} if no two vertices in $I$ are adjacent to each other. A straightforward greedy construction shows that if every vertex of $G$ has at most $d$ neighbors, then $V$ can be partitioned into $d+1$ independent sets. In particular, $G$ has an independent set of size at least $|V|/(d+1)$. Now let $G$ be the graph with vertex set $F$ in which distinct vertices $\sigma$, $\sigma' \in F$ are adjacent if and only if $D\sigma \cap D\sigma' \neq \0$, or, equivalently, $\sigma' \in D^{-1}D\sigma$. Every $\sigma \in F$ has at most $|D^{-1}D| - 1 \leq |D|^2 - 1$ neighbors in $G$ \ep{we are subtracting $1$ to account for the fact that $\sigma$ is not adjacent to itself}. Therefore, $G$ has an independent set $L$ of size at least $|F|/|D|^2$, and that is precisely what we need.
nodes.statement_short: Greedy graph coloring: bound the degree in the conflict graph, then take the largest color class.

nodes.name: $V_\phi$ (clopen basic set)
nodes.statement:
For a partial map $\phi \colon \G \rightharpoonup k$ with finite domain, let $V_\phi \subseteq k^\G$ denote the clopen set given by
	\[
	V_\phi \,\defeq\, \set{x \in k^\G \,:\, x \supset \phi}.
	\]

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement:
Since the topology on $k^\G$ is generated by the sets of the form $V_\phi$, it is enough to prove Theorem~\ref{theo:synd} with $V = V_\phi$. So, let $D \subset \G$ be a nonempty finite set and let $\phi \colon D \to k$. Let $\ell_0 \in \N$ be such that
	\begin{equation}
		e \cdot (1 - k^{-|D|})^\ell \cdot |D|^2\ell^2 \,<\, 1 \qquad \text{for all } \ell \geq \ell_0.
	\end{equation}
	\ep{Such $\ell_0$ exists since the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:endgame} approaches $0$ as $\ell$ goes to infinity.} We shall argue that $n \defeq \ell_0|D|^2$ is as desired.
	
	Take any finite set $F \subset \G$ of size at least $n$ and let $L \subseteq F$ be a set of size at least $|F|/|D|^2 \geq \ell_0$ such that $L^{-1}$ is left $D$-separated \ep{such $L$ exists due to Lemma~\ref{lemma:indep} applied with $F^{-1}$ in place of $F$}. Define a $k$-instance $\B$ over $\G$ as follows. For each $\gamma \in \G$, let $B_\gamma$ be the bad $k$-event with domain $D_\gamma \defeq D L^{-1}\gamma$ consisting of all maps $\psi \colon D_\gamma \to k$ such that:
	\[
	\text{for each } \lambda \in L,\ \text{there is } \delta \in D\ \text{with } \psi(\delta\lambda^{-1}\gamma) \,\neq\, \phi(\delta).
	\]
	Notice that since $L^{-1}$ is left $D$-separated, $D_\gamma$ is equal to the \emph{disjoint} union of the sets $D \lambda^{-1}\gamma$, $\lambda \in L$. Let $\B\defeq \set{B_\gamma \,:\, \gamma \in \G}$. We claim that if $x \colon \G\to k$ is a solution to $\B$, then $x$ is trapped in $L \cdot V_\phi$ \ep{and hence also in $F \cdot V_\phi$}. Indeed, consider any $\gamma \in \G$. Since $x$ avoids $B_\gamma$, the following holds:
	\[
		\text{there is } \lambda \in L\ \text{such that for all } \delta \in D, \ x(\delta \lambda^{-1}\gamma) \,=\, \phi(\delta).
	\]
	But this precisely means that for some $\lambda \in L$, $\lambda^{-1}\gamma \cdot x \supset \phi$, i.e., $\gamma \cdot x \in L \cdot V_\phi$. In view of Theorem~\ref{theo:LLL}, it only remains to show that $\B$ is correct for the LLL.
	
	First we bound $d(\B)$. Consider any $\gamma \in \G$. We need to find an upper bound on the size of the set
	\[
		\set{\gamma' \in \G \setminus \set{\gamma} \,:\, D_\gamma \cap D_{\gamma'} \neq \0}.
	\]
	To this end, notice that $D_\gamma \cap D_{\gamma'} \neq \0$ if and only if $\gamma' \in LD^{-1}DL^{-1}\gamma$. Thus,
	\[
		 \left|\set{\gamma' \in \G \setminus \set{\gamma} \,:\, D_\gamma \cap D_{\gamma'} \neq \0}\right| \,=\, |LD^{-1}DL^{-1}| - 1 \,\leq\, |D|^2|L|^2 - 1,
	\]
	and hence we conclude that $d(\B) \leq |D|^2|L|^2 - 1$. Next we bound $p(\B)$. Again, fix $\gamma \in \G$ and draw $f \colon D_\gamma \to k$ uniformly at random. Then for each $\lambda \in L$,
	\[
		\P[f(\delta \lambda^{-1} \gamma) \neq \phi(\delta) \text{ for some } \delta \in D] \,=\, 1 - k^{-|D|},
	\]
	and since the sets $D \lambda^{-1}\gamma$, $\lambda \in L$ are disjoint, we conclude that
	\[
		\P[B_\gamma] \,=\, (1 - k^{-|D|})^{|L|}.
	\]
	Therefore, $p(\B) \leq (1 - k^{-|D|})^{|L|}$. To put everything together, $\B$ is correct as long as
	\[
		e \cdot (1 - k^{-|D|})^{|L|} \cdot |D|^2|L|^2 \,<\, 1.
	\]
	Since $|L| \geq \ell_0$, \eqref{eq:endgame} gives the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Build an LLL instance whose bad events forbid matching $\phi$ near enough $D$-separated translates, bound its degree and probability, and apply the LLL.

nodes.name: Defining inequality for $\ell_0$
nodes.statement: e \cdot (1 - k^{-|D|})^\ell \cdot |D|^2\ell^2 \,<\, 1 \qquad \text{for all } \ell \geq \ell_0.
nodes.label: eq:endgame

nodes.name: Minimality gives $X=\Gamma\cdot U$.
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is minimal, the orbit of each point in $X$ intersects $U$, and thus $X = \G \cdot U$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality gives $X=\Gamma\cdot U$.

nodes.name: Compactness gives a finite covering set $T$.
nodes.statement: The compactness of $X$ implies that there is a finite subset $T \subset \G$ such that $X = T \cdot U$.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness gives a finite covering set $T$.

nodes.name: Define right $T$-separated.
nodes.statement: Say that a set $L \subseteq \G$ is \emphd{right $T$-separated} if $\lambda_1T \cap \lambda_2T = \0$ for every pair of distinct $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2 \in L$.
nodes.statement_short: Define right $T$-separated.

nodes.name: Finiteness of $T$ yields an infinite right $T$-separated $L$
nodes.statement: Since $T$ is finite while $\G$ is infinite, there is an infinite right $T$-separated subset $L \subseteq \G$.
nodes.statement_short: Finiteness of $T$ yields an infinite right $T$-separated $L$.

nodes.name: Each $x\in U$ lands in some translate $\lambda T\cdot U$.
nodes.statement: Consider any $x \in U$. For each $\lambda \in L$, we have $\lambda^{-1} \cdot x \in T \cdot U$, i.e., $x \in \lambda T \cdot U$. In other words, for each $\lambda \in L$, there is $\tau_\lambda \in T$ with $x \in \lambda \tau_\lambda \cdot U$.
nodes.statement_short: Each $x\in U$ lands in some translate $\lambda T\cdot U$.

nodes.name: The set $S$ of these $\lambda\tau_\lambda$ is the desired in
nodes.statement: Since $L$ is right $T$-separated, the set $S \defeq \set{\lambda \tau_\lambda \,:\, \lambda \in L}$ is infinite, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: The set $S$ of these $\lambda\tau_\lambda$ is the desired infinite set.

nodes.name: Recall the greedy independent-set bound for bounded-degree g
nodes.statement: First recall some basic facts about finite graphs. Let $G$ be a finite graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$. A subset $I \subseteq V$ is \emphd{independent \ep{in $G$}} if no two vertices in $I$ are adjacent to each other.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the greedy independent-set bound for bounded-degree graphs.

nodes.name: Bounded degree $d$ gives an independent set of size $\geq |V
nodes.statement: A straightforward greedy construction shows that if every vertex of $G$ has at most $d$ neighbors, then $V$ can be partitioned into $d+1$ independent sets. In particular, $G$ has an independent set of size at least $|V|/(d+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded degree $d$ gives an independent set of size $\geq |V|/(d+1)$.

nodes.name: Build the conflict graph $G$ on $F$.
nodes.statement: Now let $G$ be the graph with vertex set $F$ in which distinct vertices $\sigma$, $\sigma' \in F$ are adjacent if and only if $D\sigma \cap D\sigma' \neq \0$, or, equivalently, $\sigma' \in D^{-1}D\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Build the conflict graph $G$ on $F$.

nodes.name: Each vertex has at most $|D|^2-1$ neighbors in $G$.
nodes.statement: Every $\sigma \in F$ has at most $|D^{-1}D| - 1 \leq |D|^2 - 1$ neighbors in $G$ \ep{we are subtracting $1$ to account for the fact that $\sigma$ is not adjacent to itself}.
nodes.statement_short: Each vertex has at most $|D|^2-1$ neighbors in $G$.

nodes.name: $G$ has an independent set $L$ of size $\geq |F|/|D|^2$.
nodes.statement: Therefore, $G$ has an independent set $L$ of size at least $|F|/|D|^2$, and that is precisely what we need.
nodes.statement_short: $G$ has an independent set $L$ of size $\geq |F|/|D|^2$.

nodes.name: State the goal: show $Z=X\times 2^\Gamma$.
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a minimal $\G$-flow and let $Z \subseteq X \times 2^\G$ be a joining. Our goal is to show that $Z = X \times 2^\G$.
nodes.statement_short: State the goal: show $Z=X\times 2^\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Reduce to showing $Z\cap(U\times V)\neq\emptyset$ for basic
nodes.statement: To this end, let $U \subseteq X$ and $V \subseteq 2^\G$ be nonempty open sets. We have to argue that $Z \cap (U \times V) \neq \0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing $Z\cap(U\times V)\neq\emptyset$ for basic open $U,V$.

nodes.name: Get $S$ from the Recurrence Lemma (for $U$) and $n$ from The
nodes.statement: Let $S \subseteq \G$ be an infinite set as in Lemma~\ref{lemma:rec} applied to $U$, and let $n \in \N$ be the quantity given by Theorem~\ref{theo:synd} applied to $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Get $S$ from the Recurrence Lemma (for $U$) and $n$ from Theorem 2 (for $V$).

nodes.name: Pick $F\subset S$ of size $\geq n$ and set $U^*:=\bigcap_{\s
nodes.statement:
Pick an arbitrary finite subset $F \subset S$ of size at least $n$ and let
	\[
	U^\ast \,\defeq\, \bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in F}.
	\]
nodes.statement_short: Pick $F\subset S$ of size $\geq n$ and set $U^*:=\bigcap_{\sigma\in F}\sigma\cdot U$.

nodes.name: By choice of $n$, $F\cdot V$ traps some point $y$.
nodes.statement: By the choice of $n$, the set $F \cdot V$ traps a point, say $y$.
nodes.statement_short: By choice of $n$, $F\cdot V$ traps some point $y$.

nodes.name: $Z$ projects onto $2^\Gamma$, so some $x$ pairs with $y$ in
nodes.statement: Since $Z$ projects onto $2^\G$, there is some $x \in X$ with $(x,y) \in Z$.
nodes.statement_short: $Z$ projects onto $2^\Gamma$, so some $x$ pairs with $y$ in $Z$.

nodes.name: Minimality of $X$ moves $x$ into $U^*$ via some $\gamma$.
nodes.statement: As $X$ is minimal and $U^\ast$ is nonempty open, there is $\gamma \in \G$ with $\gamma \cdot x \in U^\ast$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality of $X$ moves $x$ into $U^*$ via some $\gamma$.

nodes.name: The same $\gamma$ puts both $x$ and $y$'s translates into $U
nodes.statement: Since $y$ is trapped in $F \cdot V$, we have $\gamma \cdot y \in F \cdot V$, which means that $\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot y \in V$ for some $\sigma \in F$, and since $\gamma \cdot x \in U^\ast$, we also have $\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot x \in U$.
nodes.statement_short: The same $\gamma$ puts both $x$ and $y$'s translates into $U$ and $V$ via some $\sigma\in F$.

nodes.name: So $\sigma^{-1}\gamma\cdot(x,y)\in Z\cap(U\times V)$, comple
nodes.statement:
Therefore,
	\[
	(\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot x, \, \sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot y) \,=\, \sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot (x,y) \,\in\, Z \cap (U \times V),
	\]
	and the proof of Theorem~\ref{theo:disj} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: So $\sigma^{-1}\gamma\cdot(x,y)\in Z\cap(U\times V)$, completing the proof.

nodes.name: It suffices to prove the theorem for basic open sets $V=V_\p
nodes.statement: Since the topology on $k^\G$ is generated by the sets of the form $V_\phi$, it is enough to prove Theorem~\ref{theo:synd} with $V = V_\phi$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to prove the theorem for basic open sets $V=V_\phi$.

nodes.name: Fix finite $D$ and $\phi:D\to k$; choose $\ell_0$ so the LLL
nodes.statement_short: Fix finite $D$ and $\phi:D\to k$; choose $\ell_0$ so the LLL bound holds for all $\ell\geq\ell_0$.

nodes.name: Such $\ell_0$ exists since the bound tends to $0$ as $\ell\t
nodes.statement: \ep{Such $\ell_0$ exists since the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:endgame} approaches $0$ as $\ell$ goes to infinity.}
nodes.statement_short: Such $\ell_0$ exists since the bound tends to $0$ as $\ell\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Set $n:=\ell_0|D|^2$.
nodes.statement: We shall argue that $n \defeq \ell_0|D|^2$ is as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Set $n:=\ell_0|D|^2$.

nodes.name: Take $F$ of size $\geq n$ and, via the Independent Set Lemma
nodes.statement: Take any finite set $F \subset \G$ of size at least $n$ and let $L \subseteq F$ be a set of size at least $|F|/|D|^2 \geq \ell_0$ such that $L^{-1}$ is left $D$-separated \ep{such $L$ exists due to Lemma~\ref{lemma:indep} applied with $F^{-1}$ in place of $F$}.
nodes.statement_short: Take $F$ of size $\geq n$ and, via the Independent Set Lemma, a left $D$-separated-inverse subset $L\subseteq F$ of size $\geq\ell_0$.

nodes.name: Define the LLL instance $\B$: for each $\gamma$, $B_\gamma$
nodes.statement:
Define a $k$-instance $\B$ over $\G$ as follows. For each $\gamma \in \G$, let $B_\gamma$ be the bad $k$-event with domain $D_\gamma \defeq D L^{-1}\gamma$ consisting of all maps $\psi \colon D_\gamma \to k$ such that:
	\[
	\text{for each } \lambda \in L,\ \text{there is } \delta \in D\ \text{with } \psi(\delta\lambda^{-1}\gamma) \,\neq\, \phi(\delta).
	\]
nodes.statement_short: Define the LLL instance $\B$: for each $\gamma$, $B_\gamma$ forbids matching $\phi$ on some $D$-translate near $\gamma$.

nodes.name: Separatedness of $L^{-1}$ makes $D_\gamma$ a disjoint union
nodes.statement: Notice that since $L^{-1}$ is left $D$-separated, $D_\gamma$ is equal to the \emph{disjoint} union of the sets $D \lambda^{-1}\gamma$, $\lambda \in L$.
nodes.statement_short: Separatedness of $L^{-1}$ makes $D_\gamma$ a disjoint union over $L$.

nodes.name: Claim: a solution $x$ of $\B$ is trapped in $L\cdot V_\phi$
nodes.statement: Let $\B\defeq \set{B_\gamma \,:\, \gamma \in \G}$. We claim that if $x \colon \G\to k$ is a solution to $\B$, then $x$ is trapped in $L \cdot V_\phi$ \ep{and hence also in $F \cdot V_\phi$}.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: a solution $x$ of $\B$ is trapped in $L\cdot V_\phi$ (hence $F\cdot V_\phi$).

nodes.name: Fix any $\gamma\in\Gamma$.
nodes.statement: Indeed, consider any $\gamma \in \G$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix any $\gamma\in\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Since $x$ avoids $B_\gamma$, some $\lambda\in L$ matches $\p
nodes.statement:
Since $x$ avoids $B_\gamma$, the following holds:
	\[
		\text{there is } \lambda \in L\ \text{such that for all } \delta \in D, \ x(\delta \lambda^{-1}\gamma) \,=\, \phi(\delta).
	\]
nodes.statement_short: Since $x$ avoids $B_\gamma$, some $\lambda\in L$ matches $\phi$ exactly on its $D$-translate.

nodes.name: Hence $\lambda^{-1}\gamma\cdot x\supset\phi$, i.e. $\gamma\c
nodes.statement: But this precisely means that for some $\lambda \in L$, $\lambda^{-1}\gamma \cdot x \supset \phi$, i.e., $\gamma \cdot x \in L \cdot V_\phi$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\lambda^{-1}\gamma\cdot x\supset\phi$, i.e. $\gamma\cdot x\in L\cdot V_\phi$.

nodes.name: It only remains to show $\B$ is correct for the LLL.
nodes.statement: In view of Theorem~\ref{theo:LLL}, it only remains to show that $\B$ is correct for the LLL.
nodes.statement_short: It only remains to show $\B$ is correct for the LLL.

nodes.name: Bound $d(\B)$: fix $\gamma$ and bound the overlap set's size
nodes.statement:
First we bound $d(\B)$. Consider any $\gamma \in \G$. We need to find an upper bound on the size of the set
	\[
		\set{\gamma' \in \G \setminus \set{\gamma} \,:\, D_\gamma \cap D_{\gamma'} \neq \0}.
	\]
nodes.statement_short: Bound $d(\B)$: fix $\gamma$ and bound the overlap set's size.

nodes.name: $D_\gamma\cap D_{\gamma'}\neq\emptyset$ iff $\gamma'\in LD^{
nodes.statement: To this end, notice that $D_\gamma \cap D_{\gamma'} \neq \0$ if and only if $\gamma' \in LD^{-1}DL^{-1}\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: $D_\gamma\cap D_{\gamma'}\neq\emptyset$ iff $\gamma'\in LD^{-1}DL^{-1}\gamma$.

nodes.name: So $d(\B)\leq |D|^2|L|^2-1$.
nodes.statement:
Thus,
	\[
		 \left|\set{\gamma' \in \G \setminus \set{\gamma} \,:\, D_\gamma \cap D_{\gamma'} \neq \0}\right| \,=\, |LD^{-1}DL^{-1}| - 1 \,\leq\, |D|^2|L|^2 - 1,
	\]
	and hence we conclude that $d(\B) \leq |D|^2|L|^2 - 1$.

nodes.name: Bound $p(\B)$: fix $\gamma$ and draw $f$ uniformly at random
nodes.statement: Next we bound $p(\B)$. Again, fix $\gamma \in \G$ and draw $f \colon D_\gamma \to k$ uniformly at random.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $p(\B)$: fix $\gamma$ and draw $f$ uniformly at random on $D_\gamma$.

nodes.name: By disjointness of the $D\lambda^{-1}\gamma$, $\P[B_\gamma]=
nodes.statement:
Then for each $\lambda \in L$,
	\[
		\P[f(\delta \lambda^{-1} \gamma) \neq \phi(\delta) \text{ for some } \delta \in D] \,=\, 1 - k^{-|D|},
	\]
	and since the sets $D \lambda^{-1}\gamma$, $\lambda \in L$ are disjoint, we conclude that
	\[
		\P[B_\gamma] \,=\, (1 - k^{-|D|})^{|L|}.
	\]
nodes.statement_short: By disjointness of the $D\lambda^{-1}\gamma$, $\P[B_\gamma]=(1-k^{-|D|})^{|L|}$.

nodes.name: So $p(\B)\leq (1-k^{-|D|})^{|L|}$.
nodes.statement: Therefore, $p(\B) \leq (1 - k^{-|D|})^{|L|}$.

nodes.name: Combine the bounds: $\B$ is correct provided $e(1-k^{-|D|})^
nodes.statement:
To put everything together, $\B$ is correct as long as
	\[
		e \cdot (1 - k^{-|D|})^{|L|} \cdot |D|^2|L|^2 \,<\, 1.
	\]
nodes.statement_short: Combine the bounds: $\B$ is correct provided $e(1-k^{-|D|})^{|L|}|D|^2|L|^2<1$.

nodes.statement: Since $|L| \geq \ell_0$, \eqref{eq:endgame} gives the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Since $|L|\geq\ell_0$, the choice of $\ell_0$ gives correctness, finishing the proof.
